summary: Describes operators added to the UCSB On-Line System so its users could reach the ARPANET. They are defined at level I of a system named NET and serve as an interface to the local Network Control Program. As in RFC 119 and RFC 120, each non-closed socket has a completion code variable.

eli5.summary: This is the third translator for the same site, built for users of the on-line system. Instead of writing long network code, they use simple commands that talk to the network for them.

questions: how did the ucsb on-line system access the network
how did ucsb users access the arpanet
what are completion codes in networking
subtitle: Network operators for the UCSB On-Line System

tldr.problem: UCSB's on-line system users needed a way to access the ARPANET, but the low-level NCP protocol was too complex for interactive use.
tldr.mechanism: High-level operators (functions) were defined that wrap NCP operations: OPEN (to connect or listen), CLOSE (to disconnect), SEND (to transmit data), and RECEIVE (to get data), with completion codes to report results.
tldr.outcome: Users of the on-line system could access the network through simple commands without understanding the underlying NCP protocol details.

today: RFC 121 describes one approach to making network protocol accessible to end users. The principles of hiding low-level protocol complexity behind high-level operations remain central to network system design.

sections.title: Operators for Network Access
sections.content:
RFC 121 describes operators (functions) added to UCSB's On-Line System to make the ARPANET accessible to interactive users. These operators serve as an interface between users and the Network Control Program (NCP), hiding the complexity of the low-level protocol.

Each open socket is associated with a completion code variable that identifies the socket and contains the outcome code of an operation. This lets users see whether an operation succeeded or failed and what error occurred.
sections.eli5: The operators are buttons the user presses to talk to the network. Each button (operation) has a name like OPEN or SEND, and after pressing it, a light shows whether it worked.

sections.title: The Four Main Operations
sections.content:
The OPEN operator allows three distinct tasks: CONNECT (to establish a connection to a remote socket), LISTEN (to wait for an incoming connection), and ACCEPT (to accept an incoming connection). Each returns a completion code indicating success or the reason for failure.

The CLOSE operator closes a socket and cleans up the connection. The SEND operator transmits data to the remote socket, with options to include headers and trailers containing metadata about the data type. The RECEIVE operator gets data from the remote socket.
sections.eli5: Users have four simple commands: OPEN to call someone, CLOSE to hang up, SEND to talk, and RECEIVE to listen. Each one gives back a number showing whether it worked.

sections.title: Message Structure
sections.content:
Data transmitted through these operators follows a standard format of messages, each with an op code (1 byte), a length field (2 bytes), and text data. Op code 0 means NOP (no operation), 1 means the text is EBCDIC characters to display, 2 means the text is keypresses to execute immediately, and 3 means keypresses to execute after all data is received.

A string of messages is terminated by a NOP trailer. These conventions provide a consistent structure for different types of data being transmitted.
sections.eli5: Every message is labeled with what kind of data it contains: characters to display, keys to press, or something else. The label tells the receiver how to handle the data.

references.text: Krilanovich, M., "Network On-Line Operators (Continued)", NWG/RFC 122, April 1971.
